disclaimer: For reflection and entertainment. Not professional advice.

rituals.name: Salt-Water Bowl
steps: Clean and dry the bowl.
Add the salt, then pour in the water.
Place it in a quiet corner of the room.
Say one simple wish for a calm home.
Replace the water and salt every two weeks.
safety: Keep out of reach of children and pets.
Do not drink the water.
Pour away down the sink, not onto plants.
rituals.why_traditional: Salt has long been used in many cultures as a symbol of purity. Folk feng shui uses salt water to absorb stale energy.
rituals.modern_reflection: Changing the bowl is a gentle reminder to check in on your home.

rituals.name: Citrus Peel Bath
rituals.best_timing: Eve of Chinese New Year or after a hard week
steps: Rinse the leaves or peel well.
Steep them in a pot of hot water for 10 minutes, then cool.
Add the water to a basin or bath until comfortably warm.
Splash or soak while thinking of letting go of the old.
Rinse with clean water after.
safety: Skin patch test first.
Check water temperature before use.
Stop if skin feels itchy.
rituals.why_traditional: Pomelo leaf baths are a Chinese and Malay folk custom to wash away bad luck. They are common before the new year.
rituals.modern_reflection: A warm, fragrant wash can mark a clean break from a tough period.

rituals.name: Incense Room Clearing
rituals.best_timing: After moving in, or new moon
steps: Open a window for airflow.
Light the incense and let the flame go out, leaving smoke.
Walk slowly clockwise around the room.
Pause at corners and doors.
Set the stick in its holder to finish burning safely.
safety: Never leave burning incense unattended.
Keep away from curtains and paper.
Ventilate well, especially around kids, pets or anyone with breathing issues.
rituals.why_traditional: Incense has been used in Chinese homes and temples for centuries to honour and refresh spaces.
rituals.modern_reflection: Walking through each room is a mindful way to notice what needs care.

rituals.name: Red Envelope Wealth Jar
rituals.best_timing: Li Chun or first day of Chinese New Year
steps: Fill the jar halfway with rice.
Place 8 coins in the red envelope.
Write one savings goal on the envelope.
Tuck the envelope into the rice and close the lid.
Add a coin each month as a saving habit.
safety: Keep the jar dry to avoid pests.
Refresh the rice yearly.
rituals.why_traditional: Rice and red envelopes both symbolise plenty in Chinese culture. Eight sounds like prosperity in Cantonese.
rituals.modern_reflection: Writing a goal down makes it easier to stick to.

rituals.name: Three Coin String
steps: Lay the coins yang side up, the side with four characters.
Thread the red string through all three.
Tie a firm knot.
Hang it inside a drawer, wallet or by your desk.
safety: Keep small coins away from young children.
rituals.why_traditional: Three tied coins are a classic feng shui charm for steady income. The red string is said to activate them.
rituals.modern_reflection: Seeing the coins can remind you to keep money habits steady.

rituals.name: Full Moon Water
steps: Fill the jar with water and close it.
Set it on a windowsill or balcony where moonlight falls.
Say one intention for the coming month.
Collect it in the morning.
Use it to water plants or wipe your desk.
safety: Do not drink moon water.
Keep the lid closed to avoid mosquitoes.
Use within a few days.
rituals.why_traditional: Many cultures honour the full moon as a time of fullness. In Chinese tradition the 15th day is a time for offerings and reflection.
rituals.modern_reflection: Following the moon gives you a monthly pause to reset.

rituals.name: New Year Spring Cleaning
rituals.best_timing: Days before Chinese New Year; not on the first day
steps: Open all windows.
Sweep from the back of the home toward the front door.
Wipe windows, doors and the stove.
Fill a bag with things to donate.
Finish before the eve, and rest your broom on the first day.
safety: Do not mix cleaning chemicals.
Use a stable ladder for high spots.
Wear gloves.
rituals.why_traditional: Sweeping before new year clears away the old year's bad luck. Sweeping on the first day is said to sweep away good fortune.
rituals.modern_reflection: A clean, uncluttered home makes a fresh start feel real.

rituals.name: Door Threshold Clearing
steps: Clear shoes and clutter from the door area.
Dissolve salt in the water.
Wipe the door, handle and floor at the threshold.
Wipe again with plain water.
Leave the door open briefly to air out.
safety: Dry the floor fully to avoid slips.
rituals.why_traditional: In feng shui the main door is the mouth of the home, where energy enters. Keeping it clean is said to welcome good luck.
rituals.modern_reflection: A tidy entrance makes coming home feel lighter.

rituals.name: Intention Candle

ingredients.note: colour matched to intent: green wealth, pink love, white clarity

steps: Write one clear intention on paper.
Place the candle on the plate and light it.
Read your intention aloud three times.
Sit quietly for a few minutes.
Blow or snuff it out and keep the paper somewhere safe.
safety: Never leave a lit candle unattended.
Keep away from curtains, pets and kids.
Use a stable, heat-safe surface.
rituals.why_traditional: Lighting a flame to mark a wish appears in many traditions, from temple lamps to birthday candles.
rituals.modern_reflection: Saying your goal aloud helps you remember it.

rituals.name: Mandarin Orange Pair
steps: Arrange the oranges in pairs on the plate.
Place them in the living room or near the door.
Offer a pair to visitors as a greeting.
Eat or share them before they spoil.
safety: Wash fruit before eating.
rituals.why_traditional: Mandarin sounds like gold in Cantonese. Exchanging a pair wishes good fortune in twos.
rituals.modern_reflection: Sharing fruit is a simple act of goodwill.

rituals.name: Full Rice Bucket
steps: Empty and wipe the rice container.
Refill it to the top.
Stick the red paper on the lid if you like.
Try never to let it run empty during the year.
safety: Store in a dry, cool place to avoid weevils.
rituals.why_traditional: A full rice jar is a long-standing symbol of a household that never goes hungry.
rituals.modern_reflection: Keeping basics stocked is a quiet form of care.

rituals.name: Lucky Bamboo Setup
rituals.best_timing: Any time; Li Chun is popular
steps: Place pebbles in the vase.
Stand the stalks upright and add water.
Place in the east or southeast, out of harsh sun.
Change water weekly.
safety: Change water weekly to avoid mosquito breeding.
Keep away from pets that chew plants.
rituals.why_traditional: Bamboo stands for resilience and growth. Stalk numbers carry meanings, with 8 for prosperity.
rituals.modern_reflection: Caring for a plant each week builds a small, steady habit.

rituals.name: Crystal Moonlight Reset
steps: Wipe each crystal with a dry cloth.
Lay them on a tray by a window.
Leave overnight in moonlight.
Collect before strong morning sun.
safety: Bring stones in before sunrise if they fade in sun.
Keep small stones away from children.
rituals.why_traditional: Moonlight is a gentle way crystal lovers refresh stones, without water or heat.
rituals.modern_reflection: Handling each stone reminds you why you chose it.

rituals.name: Metal Wind Chime
rituals.best_timing: Start of the solar year (Li Chun)
steps: Check the Flying Stars chart in the app for this year's sector.
Hang the chime where a breeze reaches it.
Listen for a moment and set a calm intention.
Wipe it clean each month.
safety: Hang securely, away from walkways.
Be considerate of neighbours with noise.
rituals.why_traditional: In Flying Stars (飞星, fēi xīng) practice, metal chimes are used to soften challenging yearly stars.
rituals.modern_reflection: A soft sound can pull you back to the present.

rituals.name: 27-Item Declutter
steps: Set a timer for 30 minutes.
Find 27 items you no longer need.
Sort them into donate or discard.
Take the bags out the same day.
safety: Lift heavy items carefully.
rituals.why_traditional: Feng shui teaches that clutter blocks the flow of qi. Clearing space invites new energy.
rituals.modern_reflection: Fewer things often means a clearer mind.

rituals.name: Plain Tea Pause
steps: Boil water and let it cool slightly.
Pour over the tea leaves and wait.
Hold the cup and notice its warmth.
Sip slowly, phone away.
Name one thing you want from today.
safety: Take care with hot water.
Use only plain food-grade tea.
rituals.why_traditional: Tea culture in China links slow drinking with calm and reflection.
rituals.modern_reflection: Ten quiet minutes can set the tone for the day.

rituals.name: Red Paper Gratitude List
steps: Write the date at the top.
List eight things you are thankful for.
Fold the paper in half twice.
Keep it in a drawer and reread next month.
safety: None special.
rituals.why_traditional: Red is the colour of joy in Chinese culture. Eight links to good fortune.
rituals.modern_reflection: Noticing good things helps you see more of them.

rituals.name: Mirror Placement Check
steps: Walk through each room and note your mirrors.
Clean each one.
Move or cover mirrors that face your bed.
Avoid mirrors facing the main door directly.
Place one to reflect a pleasant view if you can.
safety: Get help moving large mirrors.
Secure mirrors to the wall.
rituals.why_traditional: Feng shui says mirrors double whatever they reflect. Mirrors facing the bed are said to disturb rest.
rituals.modern_reflection: A calm bedroom view can make rest feel easier.

rituals.name: Light the Dark Corner
steps: Find the darkest corner of your living space.
Clear any clutter there.
Place the lamp and switch it on in the evening.
Keep it lit for a few hours on festival nights.
safety: Prefer LED over real flames.
Do not overload power points.
rituals.why_traditional: Lanterns mark reunion and hope at Chinese festivals. Lighting dim areas is said to lift stagnant energy.
rituals.modern_reflection: A well-lit corner simply feels more welcoming.

rituals.name: Rose Petal Footbath
steps: Fill a basin with warm water.
Add petals and salt.
Soak your feet for 15 minutes.
Think about how you want to give and receive care.
Dry well and moisturise.
safety: Check water temperature.
Skin patch test with petals first.
Skip if you have broken skin.
rituals.why_traditional: Roses have symbolised love across cultures. Foot soaks are a common home comfort in Asia.
rituals.modern_reflection: Making time to care for yourself sets the tone for how others treat you.

rituals.name: Diffuser Mood Reset
steps: Fill the diffuser with water.
Add a few drops of oil.
Switch on and set a 30-minute timer.
Start one focused task while it runs.
safety: Never ingest essential oils.
Keep away from cats and dogs, as some oils are harmful to pets.
Ventilate the room and stop if you feel unwell.
rituals.why_traditional: Fragrance has been used in Chinese homes and studies to set a calm mood for reading.
rituals.modern_reflection: A scent cue can help your mind switch into focus mode.

rituals.name: New Wallet Seeding
rituals.best_timing: Chinese New Year or Li Chun

ingredients.note: red, gold or brown are popular
an amount you are comfortable with

steps: Clear old receipts from your old wallet.
Place the crisp notes in the new wallet.
Leave them untouched for the first month.
Keep the wallet tidy each week.
safety: Do not carry more cash than you are comfortable with.
rituals.why_traditional: Starting a wallet with money is a Chinese custom so it never stays empty.
rituals.modern_reflection: A tidy wallet makes spending easier to track.

rituals.name: Stove Care Ritual
rituals.best_timing: 23rd or 24th day of the 12th lunar month
steps: Turn off and cool the stove.
Clean the burners and surface thoroughly.
Fix or replace any faulty burners.
Optionally place a sweet nearby as a traditional gesture.
safety: Make sure the gas is off.
Do not mix cleaners.
Wear gloves.
rituals.why_traditional: The Kitchen God is said to report on the household before new year. Sweets are offered for kind words.
rituals.modern_reflection: A clean kitchen supports good meals and a happy home.

rituals.name: Fresh Flowers for Harmony
rituals.best_timing: Any Friday or before guests arrive
steps: Trim the stems at an angle.
Place in fresh water.
Set in the southwest for love, or the living room for harmony.
Remove wilted flowers promptly.
safety: Change water often to prevent mosquito breeding.
Some lilies are toxic to cats.
rituals.why_traditional: Peonies are a classic Chinese symbol of romance. Dead flowers are removed as they are said to hold stale energy.
rituals.modern_reflection: Fresh blooms brighten a room and a mood.

rituals.name: Singing Bowl Pause

ingredients.note: or a bell sound in the app

steps: Sit comfortably.
Strike the bowl gently.
Breathe in and out slowly until the sound fades.
Repeat three times.
safety: Keep volume gentle for others nearby.
rituals.why_traditional: Bells and bowls are used in Buddhist practice to mark moments of attention.
rituals.modern_reflection: Following a sound until it fades is an easy way to slow down.

rituals.name: Command Desk Reset
steps: Clear everything off your desk.
Wipe the surface.
Return only what you use daily.
Face the door if possible, with a solid wall behind you.
Add one plant or crystal on the left side.
safety: Mind cables and plugs while cleaning.
rituals.why_traditional: The command position in feng shui lets you see the door, symbolising control over your path.
rituals.modern_reflection: A clear desk makes it easier to start work.

rituals.name: Red String Bracelet
rituals.best_timing: Your zodiac year (本命年, běn mìng nián, birth-sign year) or new year
steps: Ask a loved one to tie it on your wrist, or tie it yourself.
Make one wish with each of three knots.
Wear it until it falls off naturally.
Thank it and let it go.
safety: Do not tie too tightly.
Remove if skin gets irritated.
rituals.why_traditional: Red string is worn for protection in your zodiac year. It is also tied to the legend of the red thread of fate.
rituals.modern_reflection: A small band on your wrist can remind you of people who care.

rituals.name: New Clothes Fresh Start
rituals.best_timing: First day of Chinese New Year

ingredients.item: one new or freshly washed outfit

steps: Wash and iron the outfit the day before.
Lay it out with a short wish for the year.
Wear it on the first day.
Notice how it feels to start fresh.
safety: None special.
rituals.why_traditional: New clothes at new year symbolise a fresh start and leaving old troubles behind.
rituals.modern_reflection: Small changes in routine can help mark a new chapter.

rituals.name: Small Water Bowl for Flow
steps: Fill the bowl with clean water.
Add pebbles or a floating flower.
Place in the north for career or southeast for wealth.
Change the water every two to three days.
safety: Change water often to prevent mosquito breeding, as required in Singapore.
Keep away from electrical outlets.
rituals.why_traditional: Water in feng shui symbolises the flow of money and opportunities.
rituals.modern_reflection: Fresh water is a simple cue to keep things moving.

rituals.name: Write and Release Letter
steps: Write a letter about something you want to let go.
Do not edit; just write.
Read it once.
Tear it into small pieces and recycle it.
safety: Avoid burning paper indoors; tearing is safer.
If heavy feelings stay, talk to someone you trust or a professional.
rituals.why_traditional: Releasing written wishes or worries appears in many folk customs, from lanterns to paper offerings.
rituals.modern_reflection: Putting thoughts on paper can make them feel smaller.
